title: Pragmatic impairment after stroke and traumatic brain injury: Theoretical implications and empirical evaluation of a novel linguistic assessment
summary:
Human communication depends on far-reaching linguistic and mental capacities. Acquired brain damage (e.g., as a result of a stroke or traumatic brain injury) can disrupt this interaction and lead to language problems, such as in the case of so-called “cognitive communication disorders” (CCDs). These can manifest themselves at the level of thinking, such as the ability to focus attention on several things at once or to act flexibly. However, CCDs can also affect language, causing difficulties in understanding ambiguous situations, focusing on the main topic in discourse (“staying on track”) or expressing oneself appropriately in a specific situation (“getting to the point”). These difficulties can lead to limitations in everyday life for those affected and their environment. Although CCDs are relatively common in Germany, to date they have rarely been studied, and knowledge about suitable therapy concepts is still limited. 
The study is conducted by scientists from various disciplines in two countries (Germany and Switzerland) to investigate the interaction between communication and other cognitive functions in individuals who have suffered a stroke or traumatic brain injury, as well as in neurologically and psychiatrically healthy individuals.  Specifically, the study aims at (1) providing a reliable, high-quality test for detecting CCDs, and to evaluate this test instrument (2) with healthy people and (3) with people with acquired brain damage. The simultaneous testing of other cognitive functions, such as the ability to empathise with other people or the ability to process information quickly, allows to investigate whether these functions have an influence on communication skills. Finally, the effects of CCDs on everyday life are examined in order to gain a better understanding of how to cope with these disorders on a daily basis. Overall, the study aims to contribute to a better understanding and treatment of these communication disorders in patient care.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Clinical groups: 

- Traumatic Brain Injury (moderate or severe by means of the Glasgow Coma Scale <12 or posttraumatic amnesia of >1h), at least 4 weeks prior to testing
- Stroke (unilateral, first onset, verified by radiology, hospital length of stay at least 2 days), at least 4 weeks prior to testing  
- German native speakers
- sufficient visual and hearing abilities
- suspected pragmatic disorder via a short screening
- sufficient attention and vigilance functions for testing
 

Healthy controls: 
- German native speakers
- sufficient visual and hearing abilities
Exclusion criteria:
Clinical groups: 
- re. stroke: cerebellar, brain stem or bilateral stroke
- prominent neglect
- aphasia (according to patient file or formal testing)
- other neurological or psychiatric disorder

Healthy controls: 
- diagnosed neurological or psychiatric disorder
